headline: Committee reviewed revenue ideas, PILOTs, enterprise funds, CHARM facilities, and health insurance savings options for reducing the city deficit.
summary: The Deficit Reduction Committee discussed public engagement plans, new revenue ideas including cannabis revenue, harbormaster mooring fees, and PILOT agreements with tax-exempt institutions. Members also reviewed enterprise funds for the golf course, harbor, and airport, CHARM recycling facilities, municipal utilities regionalization, and potential health insurance changes including a switch to the state GIC plan. The committee agreed that paid parking on Lothrop Street is a recommended new revenue source, but most other ideas remain under research with no final decisions made.
decisions: Agreed unanimously among those present that paid parking on Lothrop St. is a definite recommendation for new revenue.
Decided against eliminating Regional Dispatch internally this year, per prior budget meetings discussion.

### THE PROBLEM AND EXPLORING HOW SMART SUSTAINABILITY INITIATIVES CAN CUT COSTS, GENERATE REVENUE, AND BECOME PART OF BEVERLY'S STRATEGY FOR REDUCING ITS BUDGET DEFICIT

- The City of Beverly faces a recurring, structural budget gap where annual expenses are growing faster than allowed revenue growth.
- The deficit is anticipated to rise without intervention.
- Growing waste volumes accelerate landfill use, increase disposal costs, and shorten landfill lifespans—adding to the City's budget pressures.
- The biggest factor controlling the cost of landfill is how well pre-landfill steps are accomplished. This is where green initiatives could help to make a difference with the deficit and potentially generate revenue along the way.

### WHAT ARE CENTERS FOR HARD-TO-RECYCLE MATERIALS (CHARM) FACILITIES?

- Centers for Hard-to-Recycle Materials are specialized drop-off centers that accept items traditional recycling programs cannot handle — things like styrofoam, mattresses, electronics, paint, chemicals, bike tubes, toilets, wine corks, and dozens of other "odd" materials. These facilities typically charge small fees and often generate revenue through user fees, sponsorships, grants, and resale of recovered materials.
- The City of Beverly does not currently have a CHARM Facility. Black Earth Compost offers residents pay as you go pickup options. The City also offers periodic drop off events for hazardous materials and electronics.

### COULD A CHARM FACILITY ADD VALUE IN BEVERLY?

- Yes! CHARM facilities turn expensive-to-dispose-of materials into fee-supported services and recoverable value, while also reducing landfill costs.
- Every ton diverted from the landfill saves tipping fees, extends landfill lifespan, and reduces long-term capital costs.
- Key Benefits:
- Fees often cover operating costs and generate surplus revenue
- Many hard-to-recycle materials have resale value and programs can sell these materials to processors or manufacturers
- CHARM facilities can attract grants and sponsorships
- Opportunity to build upon other green initiatives in the City

### CHARM FACILITIES TO EXPLORE AND RESEARCH

Local ChaRM Facility

Local Recycling centers that are not full ChaRM facilities but handle hard to recycle materials
- Gardner, MA

- Newton, MA

- Athens, Georgia
- Boulder, Colorado
- Allegheny County, Pennsylvania

- Dog waste digesters
- Construction & Demolition Material Recovery (salvaged lumber, brick, fixtures, and metals are resold)

- Solar arrays

- Green burial sites
- Battery storage facilities

- Tool libraries rental fees
- Maker space memberships

- Do more focused research on ideas the community feels are potentially feasible in Beverly

**Regional Dispatch Scenario**

Massachusetts actively provides State 911 funding for regional PSAPs and Regional Emergency Communication Centers. The state's FY2027 Development Grant program explicitly supports regionalization of 911 and dispatch operations.

There is already a relevant North Shore model: the **Essex Regional Emergency Communications Center**, which has provided public-safety communications/dispatch services under intermunicipal agreements with communities including Middleton.

Meeting with Dave Gelineau   8/5/26 ( Dave is the city purchasing agent, as well as a member of the BG&T commission.)

BG&T is an enterprise fund. Currently the management company pays the city $400,000 per year for the contract. All that money goes back in to a fund managed by the golf and tennis commission, and is used for course / clubhouse capital improvements etc.

The city does allocate approximately $17,000 per year from this money to cover city employee time supporting BG&T. Current contract goes through 2029.

The course does not cost the city anything, as any city employee time spent supporting BG&T is covered by allocations from the $400,000 fee. Conversely, the city does not make any money from BG&T, as any profits go to the management company.

Considerations:

Based on the research there does not appear to be any opportunity relevant to our DRC work. BG&T is a wonderful asset for a relatively small number of residents (full disclosure I am a member.) However, looking at this with a critical eye and from a purely financial point of view would suggest that this is a valuable, under-utilized asset. Could the city sell or lease the property for some other use that could lead to a consistent tax stream? That and other similar questions should probably be asked and reviewed in the future, maybe prior to the end of the current contract in 2029.

Harbor Management Authority:

Set up by the State, sits outside of City Government. Funding comes through fees collected at Glover Wharf, plus grant funding. Glover wharf falls under BHMA. Fees are reviewed yearly and approved by the BHMA board.

All fees collected / grants received remain with BHMA. They maintain reserves to fund capital projects related to the waterfront. Excess fees (and any fee increase) go to those reserves by State law.

The Harbormaster is separate from BHMA and is part of city government.

Considerations:

Based on the research, the only opportunity relevant to our DRC work is to verify that the city is allocating any support costs back to BHMA.

Meeting with Harbormaster Peter Dickman   8/5/26

The Harbormaster is separate from the Beverly Harbor Management Authority, and reports to the mayor. Also works closely with the fire and police departments.

The revenue (mainly fees) collected by the harbormaster go to the **City's general fund.**

Current annual revenue is approximately $125,000.

The main revenue source is permitting fees. Every boat on a mooring in Beverly must have a permit. Currently there are approximately 600 permits issued (~360 to Beverly residents, ~240 to non-residents (For comparison, Salem has ~1400 permits and Marblehead ~1800.) The fee is $7 /per foot per year, with a $100 minimum. (For comparison, Salem is also $7/per foot, Danvers is $5/ per foot, Marblehead is $13/ per foot.) The waiting list for a mooring in Beverly is 3-5 years. There are 100 or so people on the wait list.

There are also Private Guest Moorings. These are moorings that may or may not have a permanent boat. These are typically in front of someone's property, and may be used for guests etc. The fee for this is currently $100 per year. There are 20-30 of these in Beverly.

The rates are reviewed and proposed by the Harbormaster. The rates were updated last year. Prior to that they had been consistent for at least 10 years.

The city has 10 transit moorings in the harbor that are currently underutilized. The harbormaster has been working on potential plans to better utilize these moorings, which could lead to increased revenue. One of these plans would likely require a launch service, so the capital and labor costs would need to be considered.
